body.text: Soon after becoming the general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) in July 2024, General To Lam declared “a new era of national rise” for Vietnam. He also vowed to raise Vietnam’s economic growth rate to double digits from its then-current level of 7 percent. Lam quickly followed those bold statements with actions and policies that appear to set a new course for Vietnam.

First was an order for the swift streamlining of the administrative and political system in Vietnam. Under this order, several ministries were abolished or merged with others. All district-level governments were also abolished, with incumbent officials either being transferred up to the provincial level or down to the commune level, or encouraged to retire. Vietnam’s 63 provincial and provincial-level units were merged into 34 new units, a reduction by nearly a half, all within only a few months.

Moving away from the preoccupation with the socialist ideology of his predecessor as CPV chief, Nguyen Phu Trong, Lam called for making the private sector the main engine of the economy. He authorized the launch of high-profile infrastructure projects such as high-speed rail and nuclear power plants. These projects are awarded to a few private conglomerates with political connections even though they have no expertise or experience in those areas.

Lam has also been hyperactive in foreign relations, having visited about two dozen countries in the last two years. Under his leadership, Vietnam has upgraded diplomatic relationships with several countries to the highest level possible. The country seems to be doing well economically. Despite Trump’s tariffs on Vietnam’s exports to the United States, its trade surplus with the latter continues to rise.
Who is To Lam, and what can Vietnamese expect in the “new era” he has proclaimed?
“Hardman, Capitalist, and Hedonist”

The above are terms The Economist has used to describe To Lam. They are perhaps accurate, but there’s much more that we don’t know. Born in 1957 in Hung Yen province in communist North Vietnam when Vietnam was still divided into two countries, Lam reached maturity in 1975 when the civil war between the two Vietnams ended with the communist North’s victory.

Lam’s father, Colonel To Quyen, was a security agent who had spent most of those war years in South Vietnam, away from his family in the North, to abet the communist revolution in the South. He would later rise to head the Prison Department in the Ministry of Internal Affairs (the predecessor of the current Ministry of Public Security), overseeing the vast and fearful system of incarceration, which had its fingers in even the remotest corners of the country.

Trained as a young man at the College of Public Security, Lam spent his entire career in the security apparatus, rising to the rank of major general at the age of 50 and minister at 59. Family background is a major factor in career advancement in Vietnam, and his case is no exception. Given his father’s distinguished record, Lam could have been early on encouraged and prepared to aim for a higher position.

As is the case with most Vietnamese officials, certainly those serving in the military and security apparatuses, little is known about Lam as a person. Despite having ruled Vietnam for decades, the CPV still operates in a similar form of secrecy as when the party was an outlawed band of revolutionaries. At the same time, the communist regime promotes collectivism and regards individualism as a disease of decadent bourgeois capitalist societies. Ambitious officials must learn to keep their mouths shut and pretend to be humble or they will never rise to the top.

Yet Lam has had a more colorful life than most of his peers. The fact that he divorced his first wife after having had two children with her and remarried seems unusual among officials of his generation, not to mention that his second wife, Ngo Phuong Ly, is 13 years his junior. Born to an artist and an actress, Ly once trained in painting and worked as a television host. She is no doubt younger and better looking than all of communist Vietnam’s first ladies to date. Lam’s love for beauty is also shown in his private hobby to collect antiques, known to those close to him.

As minister of public security, Lam championed the construction in 2023 of the glitzy, state-of-the-art Ho Guom Opera House in downtown Hanoi. Whether Ly had any influence on this is not known, but this supposedly artistic venue is co-managed by the ministry and the municipal government, and likely the place to showcase “arts” sponsored by or at least suitable to the taste of the security apparatus.

Another, lesser known event that took place in 2017, also under Lam’s watch, was the installment of the bust of Felix Dzerzhinsky at his alma mater (now renamed the People’s Academy of Security Services). The Polish-born Dzerzhinsky, a close comrade of Lenin, was the founder of the Cheka (the predecessor of the KGB) and the Gulag camp system in the early days of the Soviet Union. We know that one of Lam’s daughters has studied in England, but can a fan of Felix Dzerzhinsky be a capitalist?

To understand this paradox we have to look at the political, social, and economic trends in Vietnam since market reforms began more than three decades ago. The contradictions found in the man in fact reflect those trends quite well.
From Grave Crisis to Half-Hearted Reform

The Soviet model, which communist Vietnam loyally followed until the mid-1980s, led to a severe economic crisis and the threat of a massive famine. A younger generation took the helm of the CPV at the time and decided to emulate Gorbachev’s reforms in the Soviet Union. As they witnessed with horror first the collapse of Eastern European communist states in 1989, and then the Soviet Union itself in 1991, Vietnam’s leaders switched to the Chinese model of economic without political reforms.

They liberalized prices, allowed private markets and trade, and stopped persecuting private businesses. They dissolved the rural cooperatives that kept Vietnam’s hardworking farmers in chronic hunger for decades. They opened up the country for trade and investment from the West and from their capitalist neighbors. They allowed Vietnamese to travel abroad, and members of the diaspora to visit.

But they have not given up state ownership of land, nor government control over major economic sectors. The CPV still does not permit private presses or any autonomous social organizations, whether cultural or political. While the economy was gradually liberalized, the government, including its constitution, laws, and key institutions such as the military and the police, adopted modern technologies to control society in more sophisticated ways. Vietnam may appear capitalist from outside, but it remains a communist country within.

More than three decades have passed since that crisis moment, and Vietnam has transformed significantly. It is no longer poor and destitute as it once was. Foreign investors pour tens of billions of dollars into the economy every year and employ millions of local workers. Rising living standards have created an urban middle class and a nascent civil society, which have grown precariously under tight police surveillance.

The annual value of Vietnam’s exports is now worth as much as its annual gross domestic product. Besides natural resources and agricultural produce, manufacturing accounts for a significant part of Vietnam’s exports, giving the impression that Vietnam is rapidly industrializing. In fact, what counts as Vietnam’s manufacturing exports relies on low-skilled workers who essentially assemble products, most of the components of which have been made abroad in countries such as China, South Korea, and Taiwan. Lam has lamented in public about this problem, and his policies to accelerate economic growth rate by greater centralization of power appear to reflect his desire to emulate Xi Jinping’s China.
A Time for Strongmen

The Vietnamese government tolerates private businesses, but, except a few with political connections, gives priority to state-owned enterprises as a symbol of Vietnam’s “socialist orientations.” After much internal debate, the CPV has permitted its members to run businesses for profit, a career that used to be considered “exploitative.” Because the state still owns all land that continues to appreciate in value, party members and their families have used their political connections to gain land use rights at marginal costs for huge profits after the land has been developed.

Since political connections are lucrative, government and party offices, which offer special power and privileges to their holders, have become commodities, now often bought and sold for thousands to millions of dollars each. Graft has pervaded the government at all levels, causing it to lose much legitimacy. While Vietnamese leaders share a desire to monopolize power and perpetuate the CPV’s rule, rival personal networks of power and wealth now compete fiercely for key positions in the party-state.

As chaos took hold and decay spread, Nguyen Phu Trong emerged in the mid-2010s as a clean party leader and an ideologue who wanted to purify the CPV and save its public image, if not its soul. Trong had gradually strengthened the power of the central party and now launched an anti-corruption campaign modeled after the same campaign by Xi Jinping in China to consolidate his personal authority.

To catch corrupt officials, Trong had to rely on the Ministry of Public Security, which has the authority and capacity to investigate and prosecute them. He also needed the police to help block the creeping trend of liberalization due to Western influence, especially among Vietnamese youth.

The Ministry of Public Security is one of the most powerful institutions in Vietnam, rivaled only by the Ministry of Defense. It oversees the national and local police, the internal security and intelligence agencies, the prisons, and local militias. With its officials advised and trained in part by the East German Stasi during the Cold War, it employs millions of people, from the village to national levels, not only those in uniforms but also undercover agents who infiltrate schools, religious institutions, artistic circles, NGOs, and diasporic communities throughout the world.

Control over the Ministry of Public Security gave Lam a powerful means of upward mobility. It is an open secret in Vietnamese politics that most officials maintain close links with certain “private” businesses, often but not always headed by relatives, who benefit from the political connections to gain easy access to land in prime locations, generous loans from state banks, monopolistic licenses for business operations, and lucrative contracts from the government. These businesses in return supply funds to the officials not only for their grand villas and children’s expensive tuition abroad but also for luxurious gifts to their superiors when promotion to higher positions is under consideration.

The officials certainly do not publicize the relationships, but the businesses must do so with their partners to obtain special treatment, rendering such relationships “open secrets.” It was thus easy and within Lam’s capacity, should he wish to do so, to discreetly collect information on those he wanted to target and publicize it when the time was right. At the same time, he can know more about his political rivals than they do about him.
The Right Place at the Right Time

Thus, Lam was in the right place at the right time, and he proved a valuable collaborator in Trong’s harsh crackdown on civil society. The arrests of even those activists who operated within the strict confines of the law terrorized the entire NGO community.

With Lam’s assistance in investigating the “open secrets” of other officials, Trong’s anti-corruption campaign netted thousands of high-ranking CPV cadres, including a few incumbent Politburo members, over the course of a decade. To catch Trinh Xuan Thanh, a corrupt executive of the oil state enterprise executive PetroVietnam, who had fled to Germany and applied for asylum there, Lam organized a secret mission that carried out a dramatic and successful abduction of the man from a Berlin park to be brought back to Vietnam via Czechia and Slovakia.

Despite his rhetoric that no corrupt officials would be spared, Trong only prosecuted those he did not like, and largely did not touch members of his own network. As the head of the security apparatus, arguably the most corrupt government institution in the country, Lam was hardly clean. Although evidence of his corrupt dealings has not yet been made public, he gained special notoriety from being seen in a viral video clip, in which Lam was fed a piece of beef wrapped in gold leaf by the celebrity chef Salt Bae at a luxury restaurant in London.

That clip prompted The Economist to term Lam a “hedonist.” But it did not end his career, largely because Trong needed him to prosecute the campaigns against corrupt officials and civil society. As Trong’s health rapidly declined in 2023, Lam made his moves against senior members of the Politburo, some of whom were more senior than himself and would be in line to succeed Trong. In the first six months of 2024 while Trong was on his deathbed, Lam was able to swiftly remove five Politburo members one by one from office.

We don’t know what really happened, but one might imagine a scene like in imperial Vietnam or China when a usurper blocked access to the palace and forged a dying emperor’s will to seize the throne. When Trong died in July, Lam was in fact next in line.

The rise of To Lam to power was not only unexpected. It was also unprecedented. He is the first police general, and the first head of the security apparatus, to assume the top position in the CPV. He had narrow work experience in a single central ministry, contrary to what the CPV’s official rule required for the position. To be sure, he could not have pulled off the whole affair without the collaboration by some other key leaders, but he appeared to have outsmarted his major rivals.

Yet he did not stop there in his quest for more personal power. In early 2025, he assumed the position of state president, which gave him formal command of the government after having secured the leadership of the party. The state presidency had traditionally been held by someone different from the general secretary, as an institutional guarantee of collective leadership. By formally and permanently occupying both offices, Lam has become the most powerful party leader since its founder Ho Chi Minh.

Having one man in charge of both offices had been debated for some time within the CPV leadership, and can be justified on account of efficiency and effectiveness. Vietnam’s leaders also look to China where Xi Jinping occupies both roles. Yet Lam’s moves to place his trusted men either from the security apparatus or from his home province Hung Yen are bound to create resentment. No less than a dozen such men (and they are all men) can be identified across various state and party agencies and in many provinces across the country.
Whither the “New Era”?

Politicians love to make promises that they may not be able to keep. U.S. President George H. W. Bush famously promised not to raise taxes during his campaign only to backtrack later after becoming president. Communist politicians in authoritarian Vietnam do not have to campaign for voters’ support and often make no promises.

Lam has been different, perhaps because of the extraordinary circumstances surrounding his assumption of office. The legitimacy gap would be too glaring without some extraordinary promises. At the same time, promising a new era of high economic growth would likely buy acquiescence among the political elites to his concentration of personal power and to his draconian policies such as administrative streamlining.

Yet Lam and the regime are taking on very high risks. By suppressing civil society, Vietnamese leaders have crushed the aspirations for a democratic Vietnam that may emerge peacefully as has happened in South Korea or Taiwan. Now that they cannot be expressed in a peaceful manner, such aspirations may be channeled into future violent confrontations.

Economically, Vietnam simply does not have the capacity to grow at double digits without creating inflation and debt. By entrusting expensive projects to a few private conglomerates with neither expertise nor experience, massive corruption, long delays, colossal cost overruns, and huge public debt burdens are hard to avoid. The concentration of personal power into one man carries substantial succession risks for the regime. Almost 70 years old now, Lam may not last for more than a decade.

The CPV will celebrate the 100th anniversary of its founding in 2030. Has To Lam brought hopes for its rejuvenation to meet the needs of a rising nation, or has he simply accelerated the process of its collapse?
